name_en: Long Feng Xia High Mountain Oolong
aliases: Shan Lin Xi Long Feng Xia
cultivar: Typically Qing Xin Oolong, as with other high-mountain oolongs
processing: Lightly oxidised and semi-ball rolled as a green-style high-mountain oolong; heavier charcoal-roasted versions are also sold.
harvest_season: Sold by harvest; spring is the usual main picking for high-mountain oolong, with winter lots also common across central Taiwan.
appearance_dry: Tight deep-green semi-rolled balls, or darker brown ones in the roasted version.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green when unroasted, amber when charcoal-roasted.
appearance_wet: Thick, supple whole leaves that unfold completely, typical of high-mountain oolong.
taste_profile: As with other Shan Lin Xi oolongs, expect floral sweetness and a thick, soft body; the roasted version trades this for charcoal and toast.

brewing.notes: Use a long first steep for the rolled leaf. Roasted lots take the same heat and can run a little shorter.

vintage_note: Fresh lots are sold by harvest and are usually drunk within a year or so, as with other unroasted high-mountain oolong. Roasted versions are a separate product that keep better; ask when they were fired.
description:
Long Feng Xia, the Long Feng Valley, is a small named area within the Shan Lin Xi tea region in Zhushan, Nantou. One seller lists its teas at 1,800 and 2,000 metres, so treat any single figure as a shop claim.

The leaf is typically Qing Xin Oolong, as across high-mountain Taiwan, made in the usual lightly oxidised, rolled form. A heavier roast also exists, marketed as bold and charcoal-toasty, and it is close to being another tea.

The specifics of its taste are not well recorded apart from seller notes, so take the general Shan Lin Xi profile as the starting point: floral sweetness and a dense texture. Use hot water and be patient with the first steep.

Ask for the harvest and the producer. It is worth comparing against an ordinary Shan Lin Xi of the same season to see what the name adds in your cup.
history: Little is documented about when tea was first planted in this valley. A Taiwanese overview lists Longfengxia among the later-developed high-altitude areas of Zhushan, alongside Shan Lin Xi, and one foreign specialist seller labels its tea under the Long Feng Valley name.
